subject: Venus planet mountains
title: There's a Planet Where It Snows Metal, on Mountains 7 Miles High

scenes.text: On one planet, the mountains are capped with metal snow.
Venus. Its lowlands sit at around 460 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Nothing should be frozen anywhere.
Yet when NASA's Magellan probe radar-mapped it in the early nineties, the peaks above about 2,600 metres glowed strangely bright.
Something was coating the peaks. In 2004, chemists at Washington University baked Venus rock in the lab to find out what.
Their answer: lead sulfide and bismuth sulfide. Metals boil off the scorching lowlands, drift up as vapour, and freeze onto the cooler peaks as a shiny frost.
Maxwell Montes, eleven kilometres tall, wears it like a snowcap. Snow made of metal, on a planet hot enough to melt it.

description:
On Venus, the mountains are capped with a frost of metal.
NASA's Magellan probe found that highlands above roughly 2,600 metres reflect radar unusually brightly. In 2004, Washington University in St. Louis chemists Laura Schaefer and Bruce Fegley showed in the lab that the coating is most likely lead sulfide (galena) and bismuth sulfide: metals vaporised in the 460-degree lowlands rise and condense on the cooler peaks, such as the 11-kilometre Maxwell Montes.
Which planet would you least want to be stranded on?
first_comment: Galena, the lead sulfide on those peaks, is the same mineral miners dig up for lead on Earth. What is the strangest weather you have heard of on another planet?
